title: Ash-Sharh: the opened chest
hookLine: did We not expand your chest and lift your burden (94:1–3)
last: AT-TIN — MADE IN THE BEST FORM.

cards: Stress has an address, and often it's the chest. It gets tight. Breathing gets shallow.
My chest is heavy, people say. I've got a weight on me. And when it lifts, when the news is good, when the fight is over, the first thing people do is take a long, full breath.
Today's surah is about exactly that feeling. It's spoken to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in hard years in Mecca, and it starts with a question about his chest.

teach.b: Surah ninety-four begins, in Pickthall's translation: Have We not caused thy bosom to dilate, And eased thee of the burden Which weighed down thy back. Sharh means opening, expanding, making wide.

In Arabic, a narrow chest is anxiety, grief, feeling trapped. An opened chest is relief, calm, room to breathe, and room to understand and accept. The surah asks, as if reminding a friend: didn't We open your chest?

teach.h: THE BURDEN THAT WEIGHED DOWN THY BACK.
teach.b: Didn't We take off the weight that was breaking your back? It's spoken in the past tense: look, it already happened. Commentators give the opening two senses.
One is inward: calm, guidance and the strength to carry the revelation.

The other, some connect with a report in Sahih Muslim: when the Prophet was a young boy, playing with other children, Jibril came, opened his chest, washed his heart with Zamzam water, and closed it again.
Then: and We raised your name, your remembrance. Commentators point to the call to prayer, where his name is said after Allah's. There's another opened chest in the Qur'an.
Musa, sent to face Pharaoh, prays: my Lord, expand my chest for me, and ease my task.
You'll hear his words, rabbi ishrah li sadri, before an exam, a hard talk, a speech.
In the Qur'an, a heavy chest can be opened, and a burden can be lifted.

how: Many Muslims recite Musa's supplication from Surah Ta-Ha, rabbi ishrah li sadri, before exams, speeches and difficult tasks, and Surah ash-Sharh is often recited in times of stress.

o: opening: a chest made wide, with room to breathe
a heavy weight that presses down on the back
a narrow gate at the edge of a town

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
p: said in the call to prayer

s: the surah is spoken to the Prophet
didn't We open your chest? it reassures him in the past tense.
an opened chest in Arabic means an injury
it means relief, calm, room to breathe and understand.
Musa asked for his chest to be expanded

games.q: Musa is sent to face Pharaoh. before anything else, what does he ask for?
o: that his chest be expanded and his task made easy
games.why: rabbi ishrah li sadri: my Lord, expand my chest (20:25–26). it's still said before hard things.

practice: Sit up, put one hand on your chest, and breathe in slowly, feeling it rise and widen; breathe out and let your shoulders drop. If something heavy is sitting there, name it, and let the next out-breath carry some of it away.
If you pray, you can say Musa's words: rabbi ishrah li sadri.

wordCard.voice: Ash-Sharh. The opening, the widening of the chest; the name of Surah ninety-four. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the opening, the widening; from 94:1, alam nashrah, did We not open.

carryVoice: Your line: the burden lifts. Some weights already have. Day one hundred eighty-four, done.
